ahmadiyya.1: Converts are embraced by a global family, with the Khalifa's name, an instant role, and hospitality.
ahmadiyya.2: Community help (jobs, housing, marriage introductions) arrives through the same structure that records your contributions.
ahmadiyya.3: Members are promised nearness to God, the Khalifa's prayers, and burial in the Wasiyyat cemetery.
ahmadiyya.4: Drifting members are visited by office-bearers and relatives; Jalsa is the annual pull back.
ahmadiyya.5: Weak sacrifice, missed duties and an unrenewed pledge are named as spiritual failure.
ahmadiyya.6: Doubts about the system are reframed as weak faith or as the influence of enemies.
ahmadiyya.7: The teaching "No compulsion in religion" sits alongside a boycott of those who leave that former members report is expected.
ahmadiyya.8: Sacrifice is praised in public, and the lapsed meet silence.
ahmadiyya.9: Aam leads to Wasiyyat, which leads to new schemes, each published with its rates; each level of sacrifice exposes the next.
ahmadiyya.10: The community's own guide calls Chanda Aam "compulsory" and other chandas "voluntary", yet says voluntary chandas are not accepted from a member who does not pay the obligatory ones.
ahmadiyya.11: Critics are cast as disloyal and self-seeking while the system escapes audit.
ahmadiyya.12: A member raising a complaint against an office-bearer becomes the problem for "creating disorder".
ahmadiyya.13: Duty rotas, dues and reporting become the texture of ordinary life from age seven.
ahmadiyya.14: Marriage, friendship and leisure are centered on the jamaat, and marriage outside it is restricted for women.
ahmadiyya.15: Family, office-bearers and the Khalifa's sermons align against a doubter.
ahmadiyya.16: Relatives and auxiliary officers carry the pressure to return or conform.
ahmadiyya.17: Community writing frames organized critics as conspiracies against the Jamaat; former members report being called misled.
ahmadiyya.18: Complaints about office-bearers are routed back into the same hierarchy.
ahmadiyya.19: Waqf-e-Nau children reaffirm at fifteen a pledge made for them before birth.
ahmadiyya.20: Shared persecution grief binds members to the institution itself.
ahmadiyya.21: Every route of complaint ends at an appointee of the Khalifa.
ahmadiyya.22: Marriage rules and purdah are framed as protection.
ahmadiyya.23: Adults' marriage, dress and reading are supervised by office-bearers.
ahmadiyya.24: Selfhood is defined by membership, rank of sacrifice and obedience.
ahmadiyya.25: Grievances are answered with calls for more prayer and sacrifice.
ahmadiyya.26: Contributions are fixed percentages of income, estates are pledged, and arrears are recorded.
ahmadiyya.27: Persecution news is framed as a reason to close ranks against internal critics.
ahmadiyya.28: Expulsion is published; former members report that a boycott is expected.
ahmadiyya.29: The system continues untouched; a new volunteer fills the post.
ahmadiyya.30: The institution publishes expulsion; former members report that members carry out the boycott.

anglicanism.1: It is present in some evangelical outreach (Alpha courses, an introductory course on Christianity run over shared meals; camps) and absent from most parishes.
anglicanism.2: Church school admissions criteria are published and can favor worshipping families (section 11), which ties a school place to attendance; pastoral help can also create obligation, more softly.
anglicanism.3: Eternal life is promised, and for clergy, a future of ministry.
anglicanism.4: Weak here: families who come for the occasional offices are invited back.
anglicanism.5: Some traditions use the language of sin, and decline is blamed on parishes.
anglicanism.6: IICSA found the church failed to take abuse seriously; that survivors were told processes had been followed when they had not is not recorded on this page.
anglicanism.7: Women may be bishops; parishes may reject their oversight.
anglicanism.8: Preferment (promotion to senior posts) and patronage shape clerical careers.
anglicanism.9: Independent safeguarding was promised, redesigned and phased.
anglicanism.10: Doctrinal breadth lets any position be "one tradition".
anglicanism.11: Critics of process are cast as hostile to the church.
anglicanism.12: Complainants were treated as reputational threats (per IICSA and Makin).
anglicanism.13: Deference to senior clergy was normalized (IICSA; Gibb).
anglicanism.14: Historically, it happened in closed camps and choir environments.
anglicanism.15: Complaints are routed between parish, diocese and national bodies.
anglicanism.16: Weak here: congregations show loyalty to accused clergy.
anglicanism.17: IICSA found the church failed to take abuse seriously, and survivors' accounts were disbelieved in documented cases.
anglicanism.18: The church was slow to respond to survivors (IICSA).
anglicanism.19: Clergy must make the Declaration of Assent to doctrine and discipline, with the house attached.
anglicanism.21: Survivors made repeated complaints that failed (IICSA); the helplessness the technique names is not an inquiry finding.
anglicanism.22: Oversight of clergy lives runs through the bishop's licence and the tied house under Common Tenure.
anglicanism.23: Weak here: a culture of deference prevails.
anglicanism.24: Clergy identity is fused with the post.
anglicanism.25: IICSA recorded evidence that some victims may have been pressured by church workers to forgive their abuser.
anglicanism.26: For clergy it is codified, working through the parish share and the tied house; for laity it is weak.
anglicanism.27: The decline narrative is used to justify closures.
anglicanism.28: Licence withdrawal ends ministry and home.
anglicanism.29: The benefice is merged and the post re-advertised.
anglicanism.30: Responsibility is deflected as "a matter for the diocese".

bahai.1: Seekers are welcomed with unity language, interfaith warmth, firesides (informal gatherings in homes where the Faith is introduced), consultation, global peace ideals, racial harmony, and the promise of a religion beyond sectarian conflict.
bahai.2: Baháʼí communities may offer warmth through firesides, study circles, children’s classes, junior youth programs, consultation, service projects, and unity-centered friendship.
bahai.3: The Baháʼí Faith offers a sweeping future: world unity, peace, racial harmony, religious reconciliation, global governance, moral maturity of humanity, and the eventual unification of the human family.
bahai.4: Someone distancing from the Baháʼí community may be gently contacted through invitations to firesides, study circles, devotionals (prayer gatherings), children’s classes, consultation, or service projects.
bahai.5: The Baháʼí Faith can devalue dissent by framing criticism as disunity, ego, impatience, covenant weakness, or failure to understand the long arc of global transformation.
bahai.6: A person criticizes administration and is told they are harming unity.
bahai.7: Bahá'ís are taught independent investigation of truth as a founding principle — investigation that must arrive at the Covenant. Investigate and dissent, and you risk the machinery reserved for 'covenant-breakers,' including shunning.
bahai.8: Service to the Faith is rewarded irregularly with appointment, delegation, or mention — institutional regard arriving unpredictably enough that active believers keep intensifying service to re-trigger it.
bahai.9: A seeker is welcomed through unity and independent investigation. Once inside, the standard shifts toward obedience to administration, avoidance of public dissent, sexual conformity, political restrictions, and service plans.
bahai.10: “Independent investigation of truth” is emphasized to seekers, while covenant loyalty and administrative obedience become central after commitment.
bahai.11: Baháʼí institutions may accuse critics of disunity while avoiding accountability for how unity language suppresses dissent.
bahai.12: A person questions administration, covenant authority, sexual rules, restrictions on partisan politics, or suppression of dissent. The first response may deny coercion: “There is no clergy,” “Consultation is open,” “Unity is central.”
bahai.13: Service expectations can become normal through study circles, children’s classes, junior youth programs, devotionals, teaching plans, consultation, and community-building language.
bahai.14: Baháʼí isolation is often soft rather than dramatic: community activities, study circles, devotionals, children’s classes, junior youth programs, service projects, administration, and unity language gradually become the person’s social world.
bahai.15: Baháʼí triangulation can run through Local Spiritual Assemblies, National Spiritual Assemblies, Universal House of Justice, community plans, study circles, service projects, children’s classes, and unity language.
bahai.16: A Baháʼí who questions administration or public dissent may be approached by assembly members, study-circle friends, service collaborators, children’s class organizers, and community members.
bahai.17: Critics of administration may be described as disunified, ego-driven, impatient, covenantally weak, or spiritually immature.
bahai.18: A member raises concerns about administration, sexuality, politics, or dissent and is redirected to consultation, patience, unity, and institutional channels.
bahai.19: Seekers consent to a faith presented through unity, peace, equality, and independent investigation, then later encounter administrative obedience, sexual norms, political restrictions, and limits on public dissent.
bahai.20: A member feels distress when dissent seems to threaten unity, then relief when they consult, soften, serve, and return to institutional harmony.
bahai.21: A member raises concerns but is repeatedly redirected into consultation, patience, unity, service, and institutional channels.
bahai.22: Administrative obedience is framed as unity.
bahai.23: Members who dissent may be treated as impatient, spiritually immature, or not understanding the Covenant.
bahai.24: The person’s identity may be absorbed into unity, service, consultation, community-building, administration, and humanity’s future.
bahai.26: Baháʼí financial control may appear through funds, teaching plans, service projects, community activities, and moral pressure to support the Faith’s growth.
bahai.27: Baháʼí communities may manufacture crisis around disunity, public dissent, criticism of administration, political conflict, or failure to serve.
bahai.28: A member who publicly criticizes administration, doctrine, sexual rules, or institutional culture may be treated as disunified or spiritually immature.
bahai.29: A member who stops serving is replaced by someone eager for study circles, junior youth work, children’s classes, or administration.
bahai.30: The Faith emphasizes independent investigation to seekers, while after enrollment dissent may be routed into consultation, unity, and administrative obedience.

buddhism.1: Newcomers arrive anxious, grieving, burned out, or spiritually disillusioned. They are met with calm voices, meditation cushions, tea, compassion language, and the promise of peace.
buddhism.2: Buddhist centers may offer meditation instruction, retreats, tea, compassion, community, trauma-sensitive language, and a peaceful refuge for anxious or wounded people.
buddhism.3: Buddhism can future-fake through enlightenment, nirvana (release from the cycle of rebirth), liberation from suffering, better rebirth, merit, karmic purification, and eventual awakening.
buddhism.4: A student leaving a Buddhist center may be told they are running from their suffering, avoiding practice, clinging to ego, or losing a precious human opportunity.
buddhism.5: Institutional Buddhism can devalue by defining ordinary desire as the root of suffering, in a form like: “You are trapped in samsara (the cycle of rebirth). Your desires are the disease.”
buddhism.6: A student says a teacher behaved abusively, and the sangha says, “Notice your aversion,” “Do not cling to anger,” or “This is your projection.”
buddhism.7: Students are told to test the teachings like gold, as the Buddha instructed — but negative findings are diagnosed as ego, aversion, or insufficient practice. The assay is welcome as long as the gold always passes.
buddhism.8: Meditation itself reinforces intermittently — some sits open into stillness, most are noise — and centers put that schedule to use: breakthroughs credit the method and teacher; dry months indicate your hindrances (in Buddhist teaching, the mental obstacles to meditation) and need for another retreat.
buddhism.9: A seeker begins meditation for suffering. Then they must attend retreats, accept teacher correction, volunteer, donate, watch attachment, examine ego, and stop trusting anger.
buddhism.10: “Nonattachment” can mean freedom from craving, but also emotional suppression, tolerance of abuse, or refusal to name harm.
buddhism.11: A Buddhist teacher may accuse a questioning student of ego while the teacher’s own ego is protected by robes, titles, lineage, and spiritual status.
buddhism.12: A student reports teacher abuse, sexual exploitation, financial pressure, or emotional manipulation. The sangha may deny it, minimize it, or say the student misunderstood skillful means.
buddhism.13: Practitioners can become desensitized to interpreting pain as attachment, anger as ego, desire as craving, and resistance as ignorance.
buddhism.14: Buddhism can isolate through sangha dependence, retreat culture, teacher authority, monastic ideals, and suspicion of ordinary worldly life as attachment.
buddhism.15: Buddhism can triangulate through teacher, sangha, lineage, senior students, retreat community, dharma texts, and the ideal of the calm practitioner.
buddhism.16: A student harmed by a Buddhist teacher may be approached by senior students: “You are attached to anger,” “Don’t create division,” “This is your projection,” “Speak compassionately.”
buddhism.17: A student reporting teacher abuse may be labeled angry, attached, egoic, unstable, divisive, or spiritually immature.
buddhism.18: A student reports teacher abuse and is told to sit with their anger, examine projection, avoid divisive speech, and practice compassion.
buddhism.19: A student “chooses” to accept teacher authority after being taught that resistance is ego and discomfort is practice.
buddhism.20: A person comes to Buddhism suffering. The teacher identifies craving, ego, attachment, ignorance, and delusion as the cause — then offers meditation, sangha, retreats, and teacher guidance as relief.
buddhism.21: A student repeatedly names harm and is told to examine attachment, anger, projection, and ego.
buddhism.22: Teachers may control students through compassion language: “We are helping you work with ego,” “This is practice,” “Your anger is attachment.”
buddhism.23: Students may be treated as spiritually immature if they trust anger, grief, desire, or moral alarm.
buddhism.24: Buddhist practice can erode identity by turning desire, anger, selfhood, attachment, ambition, and personal narrative into problems to transcend.
buddhism.26: Buddhist centers may rely on dana, retreat fees, teacher gifts, memberships, book sales, volunteer labor, and unpaid service.
buddhism.27: Buddhist communities may manufacture crisis by framing departure as running from suffering, abandoning precious human birth (the teaching that a human life capable of practice is rare), damaging karma, or creating division in the sangha.
buddhism.28: A student who reports teacher abuse may be quietly excluded from sangha spaces.
buddhism.29: A student who reports abuse leaves; new retreatants arrive and are told nothing.
buddhism.30: A sangha may say anger is welcome as something to observe, but when anger targets the teacher, it becomes ego, attachment, projection, or divisive speech.

catholicism.1: A wounded person is folded into parish life through Mass invitations, parish meals, RCIA classes (the course by which adults are received into the Church), confession, spiritual direction, saints, candles, ritual beauty, and the promise of finally belonging to something ancient and stable.
catholicism.2: Catholic parishes, schools, charities, hospitals, shelters, and social services often provide real material help: food, education, counseling, adoption support, immigration assistance, burial rites, and crisis care.
catholicism.3: Catholicism offers a massive future economy: heaven, purgatory, indulgences, masses for the dead, confession, sacraments, final rites, sainthood, and eternal union with God.
catholicism.4: A lapsed Catholic may be approached through guilt-heavy language: “Come home,” “The Church is your mother,” “You’re cutting yourself off from the sacraments,” “You need confession.”
catholicism.5: Catholicism can devalue through inherited guilt, original sin, mortal sin, venial sin, confession, penance, shame around sexuality, and dependence on sacramental restoration.
catholicism.6: A Catholic questions clerical authority, and the response is, “You are rejecting the Church Christ founded,” instead of addressing the actual abuse, cover-up, or contradiction.
catholicism.7: Catholics are taught to obey conscience as the voice of God — and taught that a conscience contradicting the Magisterium is 'malformed.' Follow conscience and you sin; suppress it and you betray it.
catholicism.8: Grace arrives through sacraments the institution meters: absolution granted through confession, communion through worthiness, blessing through standing. The peace is real, wears off, and is refilled at one counter.
catholicism.9: A Catholic confesses a sin and receives absolution, but socially or spiritually the shame remains: “Yes, God forgives, but you still need deeper repentance, penance, purity, obedience, and formation.”
catholicism.10: Catholic teaching can sound absolute in doctrine but flexible in pastoral application, allowing leaders to appear compassionate without changing the structure.
catholicism.11: Catholic hierarchy may accuse critics of attacking the Church while ignoring that clerical abuse and cover-ups attacked the vulnerable first.
catholicism.12: Clerical abuse is denied, minimized, transferred, buried in process, or reframed as the failure of individual priests rather than institutional protection.
catholicism.13: Children may be normalized early into confession, mortal sin, venial sin, guilt, penance, priestly authority, and the idea that intimate moral failures should be disclosed to clergy.
catholicism.14: Catholic isolation often works through institutional authority: the faithful are warned against secular relativism, anti-Catholic media, “cafeteria Catholicism,” Protestant error, modern sexual ethics, and malformed conscience.
catholicism.15: Catholic triangulation often runs through priest, bishop, pope, saints, tradition, family, sacraments, and “Holy Mother Church.” You are rarely just disagreeing with a local priest; you are positioned as disagreeing with the Church across centuries.
catholicism.16: A lapsed Catholic is pressured by parents, grandparents, godparents, priests, Catholic school networks, parish friends, and relatives: “Come back to Mass,” “Go to confession,” “Think of your children’s sacraments.”
catholicism.17: Critics of clerical abuse, hierarchy, or doctrine may be framed as anti-Catholic, rebellious, secularized, poorly catechized, or hostile to the Church.
catholicism.18: Abuse survivors may face layers of diocesan bureaucracy, canonical process, pastoral language, legal caution, and institutional delay.
catholicism.19: Children receive sacraments before they can understand the full theological, sexual, institutional, and lifelong implications of Catholic identity.
catholicism.20: Catholicism can bind people through guilt and relief: mortal sin, confession, absolution, penance, Eucharist, and sacramental restoration.
catholicism.21: A Catholic tries confession, penance, Mass, prayer, and obedience but still feels unworthy or trapped in recurring sin.
catholicism.22: Catholic authority presents restrictions on sexuality, marriage, contraception, divorce, remarriage, confession, and sacraments as loving moral guidance.
catholicism.23: Priests are called Father, and the Church is called Mother, creating a family hierarchy where laypeople remain spiritual children.
catholicism.24: Catholic identity can absorb the person through sacrament, family, school, confession, parish, doctrine, saints, Mary, priestly authority, and “Holy Mother Church.”
catholicism.25: Suffering is bypassed through “offer it up,” redemptive suffering, penance, confession, and obedience.
catholicism.26: Catholic financial control can appear through parish giving, school tuition, sacramental fees, annulment-related costs, Mass intentions, fundraising campaigns, diocesan appeals, and institutional charities.
catholicism.27: Catholic crisis language may center secularism, moral collapse, attacks on the family, threats to the Church, anti-Catholic media, declining vocations, or sacramental danger.
catholicism.28: A Catholic who challenges clerical abuse or doctrine may be treated as outside the faithful imagination: lapsed, rebellious, anti-Catholic, poorly formed.
catholicism.29: A questioning layperson leaves; parish life continues with another volunteer, donor, catechist, teacher, or family.
catholicism.30: The Church can say it does not control individual conscience, while also teaching that conscience must be “properly formed” by Church authority. If the conscience agrees, it is conscience. If it disagrees, it is malformed.

christianity.1: A visitor walks into church during grief, divorce, addiction recovery, loneliness, or family collapse. Suddenly everyone says, “God brought you here,” “We’ve been praying for someone like you,” “You’re home now.”
christianity.2: A church helps with rent, groceries, hospital visits, meals after childbirth, addiction recovery, or marriage counseling. Later, when the person questions doctrine or leadership, the response becomes: “After everything this church has done for you, this is how you act?”
christianity.3: Heaven is presented as the ultimate deferred reward: no more tears, no more death, reunion with loved ones, streets of gold, mansions prepared, eternal joy in God’s presence.
christianity.4: After you stop attending, the texts begin: “We miss you,” “The pastor asked about you,” “We haven’t seen you in church,” “Is everything okay spiritually?” Your absence is treated less like a personal decision and more like a spiritual emergency.
christianity.5: Christianity often begins by telling the person they are a sinner before God, sometimes this bluntly: “You are a sinner. The heart is deceitful. Without God you are nothing.”
christianity.6: A person says, “This church hurt me,” and the answer becomes, “Don’t let bitterness take root,” “You need to forgive,” or “The enemy wants to divide the body.”
christianity.7: Members are told to 'test everything against Scripture' — but arriving at a different conclusion than the pastor proves they tested it wrongly, pridefully, or under demonic influence.
christianity.8: Worship is engineered for peaks — some Sundays you leave certain God spoke to you; others you feel nothing, and the dryness is framed as your hidden sin or drifting heart, sending you back next week chasing the return.
christianity.9: You are told, “Just accept Jesus.” Then acceptance becomes baptism, church membership, tithing, serving, submission to leaders, small group attendance, evangelism, purity, correct doctrine, and never “backsliding” (falling away from faith).
christianity.10: “God’s will” is kept vague enough to justify almost anything: staying in a bad marriage, leaving a job, giving money, forgiving abuse, joining ministry, or remaining silent.
christianity.11: Churches accuse wounded members of being “divisive” after leadership created division through abuse, favoritism, secrecy, or authoritarian control.
christianity.12: A survivor reports pastoral abuse, coercive counseling, sexual misconduct, financial exploitation, or spiritual control. The church first says, “That is not what happened,” then says the survivor is bitter, unforgiving, or under attack from the enemy.
christianity.13: A believer is slowly trained to accept weekly self-denigration: “I am broken,” “I am sinful,” “I am nothing without God,” “my heart is deceitful.” At first it wounds; later it sounds like worship.
christianity.14: Christianity can isolate through warnings against “the world,” “bad company,” “unequally yoked” relationships (a believer bound, above all in marriage, to a non-believer), secular media, non-Christian dating, non-Christian therapy, and friendships that “pull you away from God.”
christianity.15: A church triangulates through “mature believers.” If you question leadership, you are sent to an elder, mentor, small-group leader, pastor’s wife, accountability partner, or “older Christian” who all repeat the same conclusion: submit, forgive, stay, trust God.
christianity.16: A pastor does not confront the critic directly. Instead, small-group leaders, prayer partners, elders, women’s ministry leaders, youth volunteers, and “concerned friends” start texting: “We miss you,” “Are you okay spiritually?” “Please don’t let bitterness win.”
christianity.17: A church labels a critic bitter, divisive, rebellious, offended, spiritually immature, or under demonic attack.
christianity.18: A member reports abuse, manipulation, financial secrecy, or pastoral misconduct. Leaders say they are “looking into it,” then weeks or months pass with no meaningful update.
christianity.19: A teenager “chooses” baptism after years of hell teaching, altar calls, youth-camp emotion, family expectation, and fear of being unsaved.
christianity.20: The church teaches that you are sinful, broken, depraved, or lost — then gives you worship, forgiveness, hugs, altar prayer, community, and “the peace of God.”
christianity.21: A member asks hard questions and is told to pray, read Scripture, submit, wait, forgive, and stop doubting. None of it resolves the issue.
christianity.22: Church leaders tell members not to date unbelievers, read certain books, attend certain events, or listen to critics because they are “guarding their hearts.”
christianity.23: Adult believers are called sheep who need shepherds, children who need spiritual fathers, or immature Christians who must submit to elders.
christianity.24: The believer’s identity is replaced with religious categories: sinner, saved, servant, disciple, sheep, witness, warrior, bride of Christ, child of God.
christianity.25: Abuse is bypassed with “forgive seventy times seven,” “God will use it for good,” “vengeance is the Lord’s,” or “don’t let bitterness take root.”
christianity.26: Churches may pressure members to tithe, give offerings, support missions, fund building campaigns, sponsor pastors, pay for conferences, and volunteer endless unpaid labor.
christianity.27: Churches may manufacture crisis through hell, demons, spiritual warfare, end-times prophecy, persecution narratives, culture-war panic, and warnings that children are being stolen by the world.
christianity.28: A church that once called someone “family” quietly stops inviting them after they question abuse, money, doctrine, or leadership.
christianity.29: A volunteer leaves after burnout; the church immediately recruits someone else and calls it “God providing.”
christianity.30: A pastor never explicitly says, “Shun her,” but preaches about wolves, divisive people, bitterness, rebellion, gossip, and protecting the flock. The congregation understands who he means.

confucianism.1: A person is welcomed into a moral universe of order, family, respect, ancestors, education, duty, and social harmony.
confucianism.2: Confucian systems offer social stability: family duty, elder care, education, hierarchy, ritual propriety, and mutual obligation.
confucianism.3: Confucian systems future-fake through social harmony: obey roles now, honor parents now, respect hierarchy now, sacrifice personal desire now, and the family or society will flourish later.
confucianism.4: A person resisting Confucian family or social expectations may be pulled back through filial guilt: “After all your parents sacrificed,” “Do not shame the family,” “Respect your elders.”
confucianism.5: Confucian systems can devalue the individual beneath role: child, parent, elder, student, ruler, subject, husband, wife, ancestor, family member.
confucianism.6: A child says parental control is oppressive, and the response is, “You are ungrateful.”
confucianism.7: Filial piety commands honoring parents — and honest speech. The child of a harmful parent must choose daily between the lie that honors and the truth that 'destroys the family.'
confucianism.8: Elder approval in Confucian-shaped families is dispensed sparingly and unpredictably; a lifetime of duty may earn one deathbed sentence of acknowledgment, and entire adulthoods are mortgaged against its possibility.
confucianism.9: A child obeys parents. Then obedience becomes career choice, marriage choice, elder care, family reputation, producing grandchildren, and suppressing personal desire.
confucianism.10: “Respect” can mean courtesy, obedience, silence, career compliance, marriage submission, elder worship, or family reputation.
confucianism.11: Parents or elders may accuse younger people of selfishness for choosing their own marriage, career, religion, or identity while using the child’s life to protect family status.
confucianism.12: An adult child names parental control, forced career paths, marriage pressure, gender expectations, or emotional domination. The family denies control and calls it love, sacrifice, or duty.
confucianism.13: Children are normalized into hierarchy early: elders speak, children obey; parents sacrifice, children owe; family reputation outranks personal desire.
confucianism.14: Confucian isolation works through family hierarchy, filial piety, elder authority, reputation, marriage expectations, career pressure, and the demand to maintain harmony.
confucianism.15: Confucian triangulation is often family-based: parents, elders, ancestors, teachers, siblings, spouse, children, family name, and social harmony.
confucianism.16: An adult child resisting family control may be pressured by parents, grandparents, siblings, aunts, uncles, teachers, family friends, and respected elders.
confucianism.17: Adult children setting boundaries may be smeared as ungrateful, selfish, immature, Westernized, disrespectful, or shameful.
confucianism.18: Adult children ask for boundaries and parents respond with silence, shame, tears, withdrawal, or “after all we did for you.”
confucianism.19: Adult children “choose” careers, spouses, elder care, residence, or family roles after years of filial debt, guilt, sacrifice stories, and reputation pressure.
confucianism.20: Family systems can bond through guilt and relief: “After all we did for you,” “do not shame us,” “respect your elders.”
confucianism.21: Adult children try to set boundaries but face tears, silence, shame, comparisons, financial pressure, and accusations of ingratitude.
confucianism.22: Parents and elders control career, marriage, religion, residence, sexuality, and family duties under the language of love, sacrifice, and harmony.
confucianism.23: Adult children remain “children” in the family hierarchy no matter their age.
confucianism.24: The person is defined by role: child, parent, spouse, elder, student, ancestor, family representative.
confucianism.25: Abuse or control is bypassed as filial piety.
confucianism.26: Family financial control may appear through tuition, housing, inheritance, business ties, elder care, wedding funding, and parental sacrifice narratives.
confucianism.27: Families may manufacture crisis around marriage, career, elder respect, grandchildren, reputation, and social harmony.
confucianism.28: Adult children who reject family expectations may be met with silence, shame, withdrawal of money, inheritance threats, or social exclusion.
confucianism.29: A noncompliant adult child is emotionally replaced by a more obedient sibling, cousin, spouse, or grandchild.
confucianism.30: Parents may say they are not controlling adult children, only advising them, while money, guilt, tears, reputation, inheritance, and family approval enforce compliance.

dawoodi-bohra.1: The community offers a warm, total embrace.
dawoodi-bohra.2: Loans and housing come from the office that disciplines.
dawoodi-bohra.3: Salvation is taught as coming through allegiance to the Daʿi.
dawoodi-bohra.4: Families pull back those who drift.
dawoodi-bohra.5: Breaches of the misaq are framed as spiritual failure.
dawoodi-bohra.6: Khatna is minimized as harmless against survivors' testimony.
dawoodi-bohra.7: An oath is sworn before adulthood and binds for life.
dawoodi-bohra.8: Favor and permissions go to loyal families.
dawoodi-bohra.9: Khatna is a "religious rite" at home and "follow the law" abroad.
dawoodi-bohra.10: No written renunciation of khatna covering every country is recorded on this page.
dawoodi-bohra.12: Survivors who speak out are accused of defaming the community.
dawoodi-bohra.13: Khatna, most often at six or seven, is treated as a family rite.
dawoodi-bohra.14: Business, marriage and burial take place inside the community.
dawoodi-bohra.15: The mother-in-law, the ʿamil and the community align.
dawoodi-bohra.17: Reformers are vilified and assaulted, per the 1979 testimony.
dawoodi-bohra.18: Litigation ran for decades before any reconsideration.
dawoodi-bohra.19: The misaq is taken before adulthood.
dawoodi-bohra.20: Shared grief (Muharram) and belonging bind members to the office.
dawoodi-bohra.21: Reformist accounts say every life event needs permission.
dawoodi-bohra.22: Permissions are framed as spiritual care.
dawoodi-bohra.23: Adults seek permission for life events.
dawoodi-bohra.25: Harm is answered with calls for loyalty.
dawoodi-bohra.26: Reformist accounts tie dues to permissions.
dawoodi-bohra.27: Outside threats are cited against reformers.
dawoodi-bohra.29: The office and the community continue unchanged.
dawoodi-bohra.30: Responsibility is placed with families and individual cutters rather than the institution; no source on this page records that framing.

eastern-orthodoxy.1: The convert is enchanted by incense, icons, chanting, fasting cycles, liturgy, beards, ancientness, and the claim that this is not a denomination but “the Church.”
eastern-orthodoxy.2: Converts may receive intense hospitality: meals after liturgy, invitations into homes, spiritual direction, fasting guidance, icons, prayer ropes, books, and a ready-made sense of ancient belonging.
eastern-orthodoxy.3: Orthodoxy offers theosis: becoming united with God, healed from corruption, transfigured into divine likeness. It is one of the most beautiful future promises in Christianity — and therefore one of the most powerful hooks.
eastern-orthodoxy.4: When someone leaves Orthodoxy, they may be told they are abandoning the fullness of the faith, the ancient Church, the saints, the sacraments, and the spiritual hospital.
eastern-orthodoxy.5: Eastern Orthodoxy can devalue through relentless emphasis on the passions, pride, delusion, spiritual sickness, unworthiness, and the need for lifelong healing inside the Church.
eastern-orthodoxy.6: A convert senses authoritarian control from a priest or spiritual father, and the response is, “That is your pride resisting obedience.”
eastern-orthodoxy.7: Converts are told Orthodoxy is freedom from Western legalism — then handed fasting rules, prayer rules, and a spiritual father whose blessing is required for major life decisions. Ask about the rules and you are 'thinking like a Westerner.'
eastern-orthodoxy.8: The convert's early months deliver overwhelming beauty — then liturgy becomes routine, and the fading glow is diagnosed as their slackening prayer rule, thickening the rule to chase the feeling.
eastern-orthodoxy.9: Converts are first told, “Come and see.” Then they must become catechumens (people under instruction before reception into the Church), fast, confess, obey a priest, adopt an Orthodox calendar, reject Western habits, and internalize suspicion of their previous religious instincts.
eastern-orthodoxy.10: Orthodoxy often says it is not legalistic, yet believers may face strict expectations around fasting, confession, sexuality, obedience, and liturgical participation.
eastern-orthodoxy.11: Orthodoxy may accuse Western Christianity, secular society, or converts who leave of pride, while demanding deep submission to priests, bishops, spiritual fathers, and tradition.
eastern-orthodoxy.12: A parishioner reports clerical control, spiritual father abuse, confession misuse, ethnic exclusion, misogyny, or authoritarian leadership. The response becomes: “You are prideful,” “You lack humility,” “You are infected by Western individualism.”
eastern-orthodoxy.13: Converts are slowly accustomed to fasting cycles, confession, long liturgies, priestly guidance, spiritual father language, and suspicion of their previous religious instincts.
eastern-orthodoxy.14: Eastern Orthodoxy can isolate converts by teaching them to distrust Western Christianity, secularism, modernity, feminism, liberalism, Protestant individualism, and “rationalism.”
eastern-orthodoxy.15: Orthodoxy triangulates through spiritual fathers, godparents, saints, elders, monastics, icons, councils, and “the mind of the Church.”
eastern-orthodoxy.16: A convert begins questioning Orthodoxy, and suddenly the priest, godparent, catechist, convert friends, online Orthodox acquaintances, and parish elders all express concern about pride, prelest, Western rationalism, or spiritual danger.
eastern-orthodoxy.17: A person leaving Orthodoxy may be labeled proud, spiritually deluded, Westernized, Protestant-minded, rationalistic, feminist, modernist, or unstable.
eastern-orthodoxy.18: A parishioner raises concerns about priestly control, confession misuse, misogyny, ethnic exclusion, or spiritual abuse and is told to speak privately with the priest — the very authority being questioned.
eastern-orthodoxy.19: Converts “freely” enter Orthodoxy after being told it is the fullness of the faith, the ancient Church, and the hospital for the soul.
eastern-orthodoxy.20: Orthodoxy calls itself a hospital for the soul while repeatedly emphasizing sickness, passions, pride, delusion, and unworthiness.
eastern-orthodoxy.21: A believer tries fasting but is still proud; tries obedience but is still self-willed; tries confession but is still sick; tries questioning and is told that questioning proves delusion.
eastern-orthodoxy.22: The Church is framed as a hospital for the soul, and priests or spiritual fathers as physicians.
eastern-orthodoxy.23: The spiritual father model can position adult believers as patients, children, or disciples whose own judgment is suspect.
eastern-orthodoxy.24: Converts may gradually replace previous identity with Orthodox convert identity: icons, fasting, liturgy, saints, incense, confession, spiritual father, ancientness, and rejection of the West.
eastern-orthodoxy.25: Pain is bypassed through humility, repentance, obedience, confession, fasting, and suspicion of pride.
eastern-orthodoxy.26: Orthodox parishes may rely on donations, stewardship pledges, candles, icons, festivals, building funds, monastery donations, and priest support.
eastern-orthodoxy.27: Orthodoxy may frame the modern West as spiritually diseased: secularism, Protestantism, feminism, liberalism, individualism, sexual confusion, and rationalism become existential threats.
eastern-orthodoxy.28: A convert celebrated as having “come home” may be dismissed as prideful, unstable, Westernized, or spiritually deluded after leaving.
eastern-orthodoxy.29: A convert leaves; another convert arrives, enchanted by icons, incense, chant, and ancientness.
eastern-orthodoxy.30: Orthodoxy can say, “We do not have a legalistic rule system,” while parish life still heavily pressures fasting, confession, liturgy, obedience, sexual discipline, and priestly guidance.

hare-krishna.1: Newcomers are drawn through chanting, dancing, prasadam, temple meals, colorful worship, music, community, and the promise of joyful devotion.
hare-krishna.2: ISKCON often offers prasadam, chanting, festivals, music, temple community, books, spiritual friendship, and a joyful devotional atmosphere.
hare-krishna.3: ISKCON future-fakes through Krishna consciousness, return to Godhead, liberation from material life, devotional ecstasy, spiritual identity, and eternal service to Krishna.
hare-krishna.4: Someone leaving ISKCON may be pulled back through prasadam, kirtan, festivals, devotee friendships, guru loyalty, and the sweetness of Krishna devotion.
hare-krishna.5: ISKCON can devalue ordinary identity by calling material life illusion, worldly attachment, maya, sense gratification, or forgetfulness of Krishna.
hare-krishna.6: A devotee says temple life is exploitative, and the response is, “That is maya testing you.”
hare-krishna.7: Devotees are taught Krishna wants loving voluntary service — and that reluctance is maya (illusion). The love must be freely given, and its absence is diagnosed, corrected, and supervised.
hare-krishna.8: Ecstatic kirtan reliably-unreliably delivers transcendence — some nights the room lifts, some nights it doesn't — and the tradition's own explanation (Krishna reveals himself when he chooses) annexes the variability as proof.
hare-krishna.9: A newcomer chants and enjoys prasadam. Then they must chant rounds, follow regulative principles (the rules against eating meat, fish and eggs, taking intoxicants, gambling and illicit sex), accept guru, serve, donate, distribute books, avoid material association, and surrender.
hare-krishna.10: Guru authority is personal devotion when attractive, institutional hierarchy when enforced, and individual imperfection when abuse is exposed.
hare-krishna.11: ISKCON communities may accuse leavers of being captured by maya while the institution creates illusion through guru idealization and spiritual hierarchy.
hare-krishna.12: A devotee reports guru abuse, temple exploitation, child mistreatment, financial pressure, or authoritarian control. The response may deny the problem or call it isolated imperfection.
hare-krishna.13: Newcomers are slowly normalized into chanting, prasadam, temple schedule, regulated diet, sexual restrictions, guru devotion, service, donations, and separation from material life.
hare-krishna.14: ISKCON can isolate through temple life, guru devotion, chanting commitments, regulated diet, sexual restrictions, devotional service, book distribution, and warnings against materialistic association.
hare-krishna.15: ISKCON triangulates through guru, temple president, senior devotees, scriptures, Krishna, prasadam, chanting, devotee association, and fear of maya.
hare-krishna.16: A questioning devotee may be approached by senior devotees, temple leaders, guru representatives, friends, and service partners.
hare-krishna.17: Former devotees may be labeled fallen, offensive, envious, in maya, bad association, contaminated, or lacking surrender.
hare-krishna.18: A devotee questions guru authority, temple exploitation, abuse, or burnout and is told to chant more, avoid offenses, take prasadam, serve, and stop associating with critics.
hare-krishna.19: Newcomers “choose” devotional life after being immersed in chanting, prasadam, community warmth, guru reverence, and devaluation of material life.
hare-krishna.20: ISKCON can bond through sweetness and shame: chanting, prasadam, kirtan, festivals, guru devotion — paired with devaluation of material life, sexuality, autonomy, and outside relationships.
hare-krishna.21: A devotee burns out and is told to chant more, serve more purely, avoid offenses, and surrender.
hare-krishna.22: Guru obedience, temple service, chanting rounds, sexual restriction, diet, and separation from material life are framed as loving purification.
hare-krishna.23: Devotees may be treated as fallen or spiritually immature if they desire ordinary family, romance, career, sexuality, or autonomy.
hare-krishna.24: Devotee identity replaces ordinary identity: servant of Krishna, follower of guru, chanter, temple servant, renunciate, surrendered soul.
hare-krishna.26: ISKCON financial control may appear through donations, book distribution, temple labor, guru offerings, festival fundraising, food service, and unpaid devotional work.
hare-krishna.27: ISKCON may manufacture crisis around maya, bad association, guru offense, material contamination, failed chanting, sexual desire, and leaving devotional service.
hare-krishna.28: A devotee who leaves may be described as fallen, in maya, offensive, contaminated, or lacking surrender.
hare-krishna.29: A devotee who leaves temple life is replaced by another newcomer drawn by kirtan, prasadam, and community sweetness.
hare-krishna.30: ISKCON can say temple life is voluntary while outside life is repeatedly described as maya, sense gratification, and bad association.

hinduism.1: Seekers are drawn by yoga, meditation, temples, music, gurus, festivals, vegetarian meals, Sanskrit chants, incense, and the promise that all paths are valid.
hinduism.2: Temples and ashrams may provide food, festivals, spiritual instruction, community support, ritual services, yoga, meditation, and guru guidance.
hinduism.3: Hindu traditions can future-fake through moksha, better rebirth, karmic progress, guru blessing, cosmic order, and liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
hinduism.4: A person leaving Hindu practice, family tradition, caste expectation, or guru-centered devotion may be told they are abandoning dharma, dishonoring parents, rejecting ancestors, or creating bad karma.
hinduism.5: Hindu institutional systems can devalue through karma, caste, purity, guru hierarchy, family duty, and cosmic explanations for suffering.
hinduism.6: A person questions caste, purity rules, gender roles, family pressure, or guru authority, and is told they do not understand dharma.
hinduism.7: Seekers are told all paths lead to the One — but leaving this guru's path shows their karma is not ripe. All paths are valid; departure from ours is blindness.
hinduism.8: Darshan of a guru or deity is structured scarcity: long queues, brief contact, occasional overwhelming moments — and the rarity is the proof of potency, funding return trips and rising offerings.
hinduism.9: A person fulfills family rituals, but then must also obey caste expectations, marriage expectations, astrological guidance, purity rules, temple obligations, and parental honor.
hinduism.10: Caste may be described as spiritual order, social custom, colonial distortion, family tradition, or irrelevant ideal depending on criticism.
hinduism.11: Caste-based systems may accuse lower-status people of impurity while protecting the moral impurity of inherited hierarchy.
hinduism.12: A person challenges caste discrimination, guru abuse, dowry pressure, gender control, family coercion, or purity rules. The response may deny that the problem is religious and call it culture, misunderstanding, or isolated misuse.
hinduism.13: Family ritual, caste expectations, purity rules, astrology, temple obligations, arranged marriage norms, and elder authority can become normal because they are embedded in family life.
hinduism.14: Hindu isolation may operate through family, caste, marriage rules, temple networks, guru communities, ritual obligations, purity boundaries, and suspicion of outsiders who “do not understand dharma.”
hinduism.15: Hindu triangulation can run through parents, caste networks, gurus, astrologers, priests, ancestors, family honor, dharma, karma, and marriage arrangements.
hinduism.16: A person resisting caste expectations, arranged marriage, guru authority, or ritual obligation may be pressured by parents, relatives, priests, astrologers, family friends, caste networks, and temple authorities.
hinduism.17: Critics of caste, guru abuse, gender control, or family coercion may be labeled anti-Hindu, Westernized, colonized, disrespectful, ignorant of dharma, or corrupted by modernity.
hinduism.18: A person challenges caste, guru abuse, dowry pressure, gender control, or family coercion and is told, “This is tradition,” “you do not understand dharma,” or “do not disrespect elders.”
hinduism.19: A young adult “chooses” an arranged marriage after family honor, caste expectations, astrology, elders, and community reputation narrow the field.
hinduism.20: Family, caste, karma, guru authority, ritual purity, and dharma can create cycles of shame and relief.
hinduism.21: A person challenges caste, marriage expectations, guru authority, or family control and is told it is karma, dharma, tradition, or parental wisdom.
hinduism.22: Family control over marriage, ritual, caste, purity, gender roles, and duty may be framed as dharma and parental love.
hinduism.23: Adult children may be treated as incapable of choosing spouse, career, rituals, or family role without elders, caste networks, priests, astrologers, or gurus.
hinduism.24: Identity may be shaped by caste, family, gender, karma, dharma, ritual role, marriage expectations, guru lineage, purity, and ancestral duty.
hinduism.25: Suffering is bypassed through karma: “This is the result of past actions.”
hinduism.26: Hindu financial control can appear through temple donations, ritual fees, priest payments, guru offerings, ashram donations, pilgrimage costs, wedding expenses, caste networks, and family-controlled finances.
hinduism.27: Families may manufacture crisis around marriage, caste, astrology, ritual neglect, family honor, gender roles, or guru criticism.
hinduism.28: A person who rejects caste expectations, arranged marriage, ritual duty, or guru authority may be treated as dishonoring family or abandoning dharma.
hinduism.29: A child who rejects arranged expectations may be replaced emotionally by a sibling or cousin who obeys.
hinduism.30: Families may say marriage choices are voluntary, while caste, astrology, parental honor, inheritance, and community reputation make refusal devastating.

indigenous.1: People may be drawn through ceremony, ancestry, land, elders, songs, healing rituals, initiation, and the promise of returning to what colonization or modernity stole.
indigenous.2: Indigenous, folk, and ancestral traditions may offer ceremony, healing, elder guidance, songs, land connection, initiation, family belonging, and recovery of identity after displacement or colonization.
indigenous.3: Indigenous, folk, and ancestral systems can future-fake through ancestral blessing, restored identity, healing of bloodlines, land reconnection, initiation, protection, fertility, communal restoration, and return to original ways.
indigenous.4: Someone leaving ancestral, folk, or Indigenous religious practice may be pulled back through elders, family, initiation obligations, ancestral fear, land connection, or claims of spiritual protection.
indigenous.5: Indigenous, folk, and ancestral systems can devalue through lineage obligation, ancestral fear, elder authority, ritual purity, initiation hierarchy, and belonging anxiety.
indigenous.6: A person questions an elder, healer, shaman, ritual authority, or family tradition, and is told they are disrespecting the ancestors.
indigenous.7: Reconnecting descendants are told the tradition is their birthright — and that questioning an elder's demands proves colonization has claimed their mind. Their heritage is inside; their judgment must wait outside.
indigenous.8: Where divination is practiced, readings can pay out intermittently — some land, most are ambiguous — and landing readings can become the practitioner's reputation while ambiguous ones become the client's unreadiness.
indigenous.9: A reconnecting person begins with ceremony or family practice. Then they must accept elder authority, secrecy, offerings, initiation, ancestral obligations, ritual payments, and silence around concerns.
indigenous.10: “Respecting ancestors” can mean remembrance, ritual participation, secrecy, obedience to elders, payments, initiation, or silence.
indigenous.11: Elders, shamans, healers, or ritual authorities may accuse dissenters of disrespecting ancestors while using ancestor language to protect their own authority.
indigenous.12: A person reports abuse, exploitation, sexual coercion, financial pressure, ritual harm, or elder misconduct. The response may deny it or say outsiders cannot understand sacred ways.
indigenous.13: Reconnecting people may be normalized into elder authority, ritual secrecy, offerings, initiation, spirit fear, ancestral obligation, and silence around internal problems.
indigenous.14: Indigenous, folk, and ancestral systems can isolate through elders, initiations, secrecy, ritual obligations, family lineage, land connection, spirit fear, and claims that outsiders cannot understand.
indigenous.15: Indigenous, folk, and ancestral traditions can triangulate through elders, ancestors, spirits, land, clan, family, initiation, healers, shamans, ritual obligations, and community survival.
indigenous.16: A person questioning an elder, healer, shaman, family ritual, or ancestral obligation may be pressured by relatives, initiates, community elders, ritual assistants, or spiritual peers.
indigenous.17: A person who questions elders, healers, shamans, payments, rituals, secrecy, or abuse may be labeled colonized, disrespectful, disconnected, cursed, spiritually dangerous, inauthentic, or betraying ancestors.
indigenous.18: A person questions an elder, healer, shaman, ritual demand, payment, secrecy, or abuse and is told outsiders cannot understand.
indigenous.19: A reconnecting person “chooses” initiation, offerings, secrecy, elder obedience, or ritual obligations after being told the ancestors are calling.
indigenous.20: A person is told they are disconnected, cursed, unprotected, colonized, or neglecting ancestors — then relief comes through ceremony, offerings, elder approval, initiation, or secrecy.
indigenous.21: A person questions an elder, ritual, payment, initiation, or secrecy and is told they are disrespectful, colonized, cursed, or disconnected.
indigenous.22: Elders, healers, shamans, or ritual authorities may control through ancestry, spirits, secrecy, initiation, offerings, and protection language.
indigenous.23: Elders, healers, shamans, or ritual authorities may treat younger or reconnecting people as too ignorant to question.
indigenous.24: Reconnecting people may have identity rebuilt around ancestors, land, bloodline, spirits, elders, initiation, secrecy, and ritual obligation.
indigenous.25: Abuse by elders or healers may be bypassed as initiation, testing, cleansing, ancestral demand, or sacred secrecy.
indigenous.26: Financial control may appear through offerings, initiation fees, healer payments, ritual materials, travel, secrecy obligations, ceremony costs, and elder support.
indigenous.27: Manufactured crisis may appear through warnings of angry ancestors, spirit attack, curses, broken taboos, failed rituals, land displeasure, or loss of protection.
indigenous.28: A person who questions elders, ceremonies, payments, secrecy, or abuse may be labeled disrespectful, colonized, disconnected, cursed, or spiritually dangerous.
indigenous.29: A reconnecting person who questions elders may be replaced by another seeker more hungry for belonging.
indigenous.30: Elders or healers may say initiation, payment, secrecy, or obedience is voluntary, while refusal is framed as disrespecting ancestors or losing protection.

islam.1: A new convert may be celebrated by the local Muslim community with hugs, meals, gifts, Arabic phrases, invitations to iftar, and declarations that they are now part of the ummah (the worldwide community of Muslims).
islam.2: A new Muslim may receive meals, gifts, Qurans, clothing, Arabic lessons, help with prayer, invitations to iftar, marriage introductions, and social protection from the ummah.
islam.3: Islam offers paradise as the ultimate deferred reward: gardens, rivers, peace, purified companionship, divine pleasure, safety from hell, reunion, and eternal success.
islam.4: A Muslim who distances from the mosque or from Islam may be contacted by family, friends, elders, or community members: “Come back to salah,” “Don’t forget Allah,” “The dunya is distracting you.” (Salah is the ritual prayer; the dunya is worldly life.)
islam.5: Institutional Islam can devalue by emphasizing human weakness, forgetfulness, ingratitude, and need for divine guidance. Verses such as “man was created weak” (Qur’an 4:28) and “man is ungrateful to his Lord” (100:6) are scripture; the institutional move is to use them as a standing verdict on the believer rather than a call to humility.
islam.6: A Muslim questions a rule and is told, “You are following your desires,” “Your iman is weak,” or “Shaytan is whispering to you.”
islam.7: A questioning Muslim is told Islam commands the pursuit of knowledge — but the conclusions are pre-approved. Seek and stop short: lazy. Seek and arrive elsewhere: misguided, whispered-to by Shaytan.
islam.8: The sweetness of iman is taught as attainable and elusive — felt in Ramadan, gone by Muharram (the first month of the Islamic year) — and its absence is read as your sins hardening the heart, driving intensified practice to recover a feeling the community defines.
islam.9: A convert is first celebrated for saying the shahada (the declaration of faith). Then the expectations escalate: pray correctly, learn Arabic sounds, dress properly, fast, avoid old holidays, change friendships, marry appropriately, and stop questioning.
islam.10: “There is no compulsion in religion” may be quoted publicly, while family, community, gender, and apostasy pressures make exit socially dangerous.
islam.11: Islamic authorities may accuse critics of arrogance before Allah while demanding obedience to human clerics, family systems, gender rules, and communal norms.
islam.12: A person reports abuse by an imam, teacher, spouse, family elder, or community leader. The response may be denial, then accusations of slander, fitna, dishonoring the ummah, or helping enemies of Islam.
islam.13: A convert gradually accepts increasing regulation: prayer times, Arabic recitation, halal food, Ramadan fasting, gender norms, dress codes, mosque expectations, and family/community scrutiny.
islam.14: Islam can isolate through the concept of the ummah as primary belonging and through warnings against dunya, haram environments, non-Muslim influence, immodest spaces, alcohol culture, dating culture, and secular morality.
islam.15: Islam can triangulate through family, imam, mosque, Qur’an teacher, spouse, children, ummah, ancestors, and fear of outsiders.
islam.16: A Muslim who questions Islam or mosque authority may be approached by parents, siblings, aunties, uncles, imams, spouses, and community members: “Come back to salah,” “Don’t embarrass the family,” “You’re being influenced.”
islam.17: Apostates or critics may be labeled arrogant, corrupted by the West, Islamophobic, traumatized, attention-seeking, immoral, or following desires.
islam.18: A person reports abuse by an imam, teacher, husband, elder, or family member and is told to be patient, avoid fitna, preserve family honor, or not damage the ummah.
islam.19: A convert says the shahada in a warm community setting, then later discovers the social expectations around prayer, fasting, dress, marriage, family, gender, and apostasy.
islam.20: The believer is taught fear of hell, the grave, Judgment Day, divine displeasure, and dying outside submission — then receives relief through prayer, fasting, repentance, Qur’an, mosque community, Ramadan, and the ummah.
islam.21: A person asks about fear, gender pressure, family control, or doubt and is told to increase iman, make duʿa, be patient, and avoid Shaytan.
islam.22: Families and communities may control clothing, marriage, friendships, prayer, fasting, and public behavior while saying they are protecting faith, honor, modesty, and akhirah.
islam.23: Adults may be treated as morally unsafe without family, imam, scholar, or community oversight.
islam.24: Muslim identity can reorganize the entire self: name, dress, diet, daily schedule, prayer, gender interaction, family life, speech, sexuality, marriage, politics, and social belonging.
islam.25: Abuse or family control may be bypassed with sabr (patience), duʿa, qadar (divine decree), “Allah tests those He loves,” or “Allah knows best.”
islam.26: Islamic communities may use zakat, sadaqah, mosque donations, madrasa fees, Islamic school tuition, charity drives, and fundraising dinners.
islam.27: Islamic communities may manufacture crisis through fears of hell, apostasy, Western corruption, fitna, family dishonor, moral collapse, Islamophobia, and children losing Islam.
islam.28: A Muslim who doubts, removes hijab, leaves prayer, dates outside expectation, or questions Islam may be treated as spiritually dangerous.
islam.29: A convert who leaves is replaced emotionally by a new shahada story.
islam.30: A mosque or family may say hijab is a choice while making removal socially devastating.

jainism.1: A seeker is drawn by radical nonviolence, vegetarianism, discipline, meditation, simplicity, and the moral seriousness of ahimsa.
jainism.2: Jain communities may offer support through food, business networks, family systems, temple life, education, ritual events, and ethical community.
jainism.3: Jainism offers liberation from karma, escape from rebirth, purity of soul, nonviolence, and eventual release through discipline.
jainism.4: A Jain leaving strict practice may be told they are accumulating karma, abandoning ahimsa, becoming spiritually careless, or dishonoring family discipline.
jainism.5: Jainism can devalue through impossible purity. Ordinary human life constantly causes harm: eating, moving, working, desiring, consuming, owning, and surviving all carry moral weight.
jainism.6: Someone says fasting or purity expectations are harming them, and the response is, “You are attached to the body.”
jainism.7: Jains are taught radical nonviolence including speech — so naming a teacher's harm 'violently' is itself a violation. Gentle naming is ignored; forceful naming is himsa (violence, the opposite of ahimsa).
jainism.8: Austerity is publicly honored on an irregular schedule — the eight-day faster celebrated at one Paryushana and unnoticed the next year — and households chase the community's shifting attention with escalating vows.
jainism.9: A Jain follows vegetarianism. Then stricter expectations appear: no root vegetables, fasting, festival vows, purity rules, temple attendance, monk reverence, and public restraint.
jainism.10: Dietary rules may be framed as personal discipline, family expectation, karmic necessity, compassion, or purity depending on the audience.
jainism.11: Jain communities may accuse people of violence for relaxing dietary rules while ignoring emotional violence caused by shame, purity ranking, and moral pressure.
jainism.12: A person says fasting pressure, purity expectations, food shame, or family control harmed them. The response may deny harm and frame the concern as lack of discipline.
jainism.13: Dietary restriction can escalate from vegetarianism to stricter rules, fasting, festival vows, avoidance of root vegetables, purity concerns, and shame around ordinary eating.
jainism.14: Jain isolation can happen through strict dietary rules, fasting culture, temple community, marriage expectations, business networks, family honor, and moral ranking around purity.
jainism.15: Jain triangulation works through family, temple community, monks, nuns, dietary rules, fasting culture, karma, purity, and moral comparison.
jainism.16: A Jain who loosens dietary restrictions or stops fasting may be pressured by parents, relatives, temple members, monks, nuns, and community friends.
jainism.17: A person who stops fasting or relaxes dietary restriction may be smeared as indulgent, violent, impure, attached, lazy, or spiritually careless.
jainism.18: A person says fasting, food shame, or purity pressure is harming them and is told they are attached to the body.
jainism.19: A person “chooses” strict diet after family, temple, karma, purity, and comparison to ascetics make ordinary eating feel morally contaminated.
jainism.20: Jain practice can create cycles of purity anxiety and relief: food rules, fasting, restraint, karma, harm, and moral contamination.
jainism.21: A person tries to relax food rules, stop fasting, or care for their body and is told they are attached, impure, violent, or karmically careless.
jainism.22: Food restrictions, fasting, restraint, and purity rules are framed as compassion for all life.
jainism.23: Adults may be corrected like children over food, fasting, purity, temple attendance, and restraint.
jainism.24: The person may become defined by purity, restraint, diet, fasting, harm avoidance, karma reduction, and moral discipline.
jainism.25: Bodily harm from fasting or strict practice may be bypassed as detachment.
jainism.26: Jain financial control may appear through temple donations, festival sponsorships, monk/nun support, charity, wedding costs, business networks, and prestige around giving.
jainism.27: Jain communities may manufacture crisis around food, fasting, purity, karma, ritual failure, and harm to living beings.
jainism.28: Someone who relaxes dietary rules, stops fasting, or questions purity pressure may be treated as indulgent, careless, violent, or spiritually weak.
jainism.29: A person who stops fasting is replaced in moral esteem by stricter relatives or ascetics.
jainism.30: Strict food rules and fasting are said to be voluntary, but family and community shame make refusal morally costly.

jehovahs-witnesses.1: A lonely or grieving person receives repeated home visits, Bible studies, patient attention, and a ready-made explanation for why the world is falling apart.
jehovahs-witnesses.2: Jehovah’s Witnesses may offer repeated home visits, Bible studies, transportation, friendship, congregation meals, help during illness, and a ready-made explanation for world chaos.
jehovahs-witnesses.3: Jehovah’s Witnesses future-fake through the imminent paradise earth: no sickness, no death, resurrected loved ones, peace, abundance, and life after Armageddon.
jehovahs-witnesses.4: When a Witness drifts, elders may visit, call, write letters, or request a shepherding call (a pastoral visit by elders); family guilt and the line “Jehovah is waiting for your return” carry the rest.
jehovahs-witnesses.5: Jehovah’s Witnesses can devalue through constant contrast between Jehovah’s organization and the wicked world.
jehovahs-witnesses.6: A Witness questions the Governing Body and is told independent thinking is dangerous.
jehovahs-witnesses.7: Witnesses are urged to make the truth their own through personal study — using only Watch Tower publications. Independent research is 'spiritual pornography.' Study is mandatory; studying is forbidden.
jehovahs-witnesses.8: Congregational standing is continuously variable — commendation from the platform, 'encouragement' visits, privileges extended and quietly removed — recalculated from monthly field-service reports (hours for pioneers; since November 2023 only whether they took part for other publishers) and meeting attendance.
jehovahs-witnesses.9: A Bible student starts with study. Then comes meeting attendance, field service, baptism, no holidays, no birthdays, no blood transfusions, loyalty to the Governing Body, and shunning compliance.
jehovahs-witnesses.10: “New light” allows past doctrines to be treated as mandatory at the time but replaceable later without institutional accountability.
jehovahs-witnesses.11: Jehovah’s Witnesses may accuse ex-members of being apostate, bitter, proud, or influenced by Satan while avoiding accountability for shunning, failed predictions, blood policy harm, and abuse handling.
jehovahs-witnesses.12: A Witness questions shunning, failed predictions, blood transfusion policy, child abuse handling, or Governing Body authority. The organization denies wrongdoing or says critics distort the truth.
jehovahs-witnesses.13: Witnesses are normalized into meetings, field service, no holidays, no birthdays, no political participation, no blood transfusions, and suspicion of “the world.”
jehovahs-witnesses.14: Jehovah’s Witnesses isolate explicitly through warnings against “the world,” apostates, higher education, holidays, non-Witness friendships, independent thinking, and outside religious or political involvement.
jehovahs-witnesses.15: Jehovah’s Witnesses triangulate through elders, Governing Body, family, congregation, field service groups, judicial committees, and Armageddon fear.
jehovahs-witnesses.16: A drifting Witness may receive elder visits, family pressure, congregation monitoring, shepherding calls, and reminders about meetings, field service, Armageddon, and paradise.
jehovahs-witnesses.17: Ex-members may be labeled apostate, mentally diseased, bitter, proud, satanic, dangerous, or bad association.
jehovahs-witnesses.18: A member questions failed predictions, shunning, abuse handling, blood doctrine, or Governing Body authority and is told to wait on Jehovah.
jehovahs-witnesses.19: A person “chooses” baptism after social life, family approval, paradise hope, and Armageddon survival are tied to organizational loyalty.
jehovahs-witnesses.20: Witnesses are bonded through Armageddon fear, paradise hope, shunning, meetings, field service, and organizational loyalty.
jehovahs-witnesses.21: A Witness questions doctrine or policy and is told to wait on Jehovah, avoid apostate material, trust the Governing Body, and stay loyal.
jehovahs-witnesses.22: Shunning is framed as loving discipline.
jehovahs-witnesses.23: Members are treated as spiritually unsafe without the Governing Body’s direction.
jehovahs-witnesses.24: Witness identity reorganizes life around meetings, field service, Governing Body direction, paradise hope, Armageddon, no holidays, no birthdays, no political involvement, and separation from “the world.”
jehovahs-witnesses.25: Failed predictions are bypassed with “new light.”
jehovahs-witnesses.26: Jehovah’s Witnesses may use donations, unpaid construction labor, field service, meeting attendance, literature distribution, and organizational volunteering.
jehovahs-witnesses.27: Jehovah’s Witnesses may manufacture crisis through Armageddon urgency, apostate fear, Satan’s world, bad association, blood doctrine, meeting attendance, and field service.
jehovahs-witnesses.28: Disfellowshipping and disassociation can produce direct social discard through shunning.
